title: The Ring of Gyges
text:
In Plato's Republic, Glaucon challenges Socrates to prove that justice is worth having for its own sake. To make his case, he tells a story about Gyges, a shepherd in the service of the king of Lydia.

One day, after a storm and an earthquake, the ground split open where Gyges was grazing his flock. He went down into the chasm and found a hollow bronze horse with little doors. Inside lay the body of a man larger than human size, wearing nothing but a gold ring. Gyges took the ring and went back up.

At the monthly meeting of the shepherds, he happened to turn the setting of the ring toward the inside of his hand and found that the others began talking about him as if he had gone. He turned it back and became visible again. Once he was sure of its power, he arranged to be one of the messengers sent to the king. At the palace he seduced the queen, plotted with her, killed the king and took the throne.

Glaucon's argument is that if there were two such rings, one worn by a just man and one by an unjust man, both would end up doing the same. People are just, he says, only because they fear being caught. Socrates spends much of the rest of the Republic trying to prove him wrong.
lesson: Ask yourself what you would do if no one could ever find out. Character is built in exactly those moments, especially as you gain power and fewer people can check you.
location: Athens, Greece (story set in Lydia, modern Turkey)
